name: Subject–Verb Agreement
summary: Matching the verb to the real subject of the sentence.

paragraphs: Every sentence in English has two key parts: a subject, which tells us who or what the sentence is about, and a verb, which tells us what that subject does or is. Subject–verb agreement means these two parts must match in number. If the subject is one thing, the verb takes its singular form. If the subject is more than one thing, the verb takes its plural form.

The rule itself is simple. The challenge is that real sentences are rarely as short as “The bus is late.” In academic writing, subjects get longer, extra words appear between the subject and the verb, and some nouns look plural when they are actually singular. This page shows you how to find the real subject every time, so choosing the verb is never a guess.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: One subject → singular verb. More than one → plural verb.

paragraphs: Subject–verb agreement appears in almost every sentence you write, which makes it one of the first things an examiner notices. A single slip in a long essay will not do much damage. But when the same mistake appears again and again, it signals that your grammar is not fully under control, and that affects your Grammatical Range and Accuracy score.
The good news is that this is one of the most fixable errors in IELTS writing. Once you know where to look, you can find and correct it in seconds during your final check.

Here is something most learners use every day without noticing. In the present simple, the letter -s does two opposite jobs. On a noun, -s usually means more than one: one student, two students. On a verb, -s means only one: he studies, they study.
So in a basic sentence, the -s sits on one side only, either on the noun or on the verb, but never on both. Think of a see-saw: when one side goes up, the other side comes down.

Not every verb form changes with the subject, which makes your job easier. Only a small group of verbs needs your attention: present simple verbs, and the verbs be and have. These are the ones to check carefully in every sentence you write.

blocks.title: The safe zone
blocks.text: Apart from was and were, past simple verbs (worked, went, increased) never change, and neither do modal verbs (can, will, should, must, may). “The student can…” and “The students can…” are both correct. This means most agreement errors happen with is/are, was/were, has/have and present simple verbs.

paragraphs: Before we look at the rules, it helps to give names to the two parts of a long subject. Once you can separate them, most agreement problems simply disappear.

rows: The main noun that the subject is built around. The verb agrees with this word.
The extra words attached to the head noun that add detail. They often begin with of, in, with, for, who, which or that.
The price of vegetables → of vegetables

sections.title: Rule 1: Find the head noun, ignore the modifier
sections.label: Rule 1: Find the head noun, ignore the modifier

paragraphs: Imagine you are writing “The price of vegetables…” and you reach the verb. The last word you wrote was vegetables, a plural noun, so your instinct says have. But vegetables is only part of the modifier. The sentence is really about the price, and price is singular, so the correct verb is has.
This is the most common agreement error in IELTS writing, because academic subjects are often long. The longer the modifier, the easier it is to lose track of the head noun.

items.text: The price of vegetables have gone up.
The price of vegetables has gone up.
The quality of roads in rural areas are poor.
The quality of roads in rural areas is poor.

rows: The number of cars in the city

blocks.title: Try this
blocks.text: Cover the modifier with your finger and read the head noun and the verb together. “The price… has” sounds right. “The price… have” does not.

sections.title: Rule 2: Two subjects joined by and are plural
sections.label: Rule 2: Two subjects joined by and are plural

paragraphs: When two subjects are joined by and, you are talking about two separate things at the same time, so the verb must be plural. This is true even when each item on its own is singular. One brother is singular, and one sister is singular, but a brother and a sister together are two people.
The common mistake here is to look only at the noun closest to the verb, which is often singular, and choose a singular verb by accident.

items.text: My brother and my sister lives abroad.
My brother and my sister live abroad.
Poor diet and lack of exercise is major causes of obesity.
Poor diet and lack of exercise are major causes of obesity.

sections.title: Rule 3: Each, every, everyone and one of are singular
sections.label: Rule 3: Each, every, everyone and one of are singular

paragraphs: Words like everyone and every student make us picture a whole group of people, so our instinct often says plural. Grammatically, however, these words look at the group one person at a time. That is why they always take a singular verb.

One of works in the same way. You may be talking about a group (one of my friends), but the subject is the single person or thing you pick out of that group. The plural noun after of is only part of the modifier.

rows: Each of the students has a laptop.
Every student has a lab partner.
Everyone in my family uses WhatsApp.
One of my friends is a doctor.

items.text: One of the main reasons are cost.
One of the main reasons is cost.

paragraphs: Some nouns cannot be counted, so they have no plural form. You cannot say two informations or three traffics. Because these nouns are always treated as one single mass, they always take a singular verb.
Many uncountable nouns are very common in IELTS essays, especially when you write about technology, the environment, education or the economy. It is worth learning the most frequent ones by topic.

items.text: The information on this website are wrong.
The information on this website is wrong.
Traffic in big cities is getting worse every year.

sections.title: Rule 5: Words that trick your eyes
sections.label: Rule 5: Words that trick your eyes

paragraphs: Spelling can mislead you with a small group of nouns. Some end in -s but are singular, usually because they name a subject of study or a single body of information. Others have no -s at all but are plural, because they already refer to a group of people.
There is no shortcut here: these words simply need to be learned. Fortunately, the list is short, and the same words appear again and again in IELTS topics.

items.text: The news was shocking.
Economics is a popular subject at university.
People are worried about rising prices.
The police are investigating the case.

paragraphs: Sometimes the subject of a sentence is not a person or an object but an activity, such as learning a language or using public transport. However many nouns appear inside that activity, the activity itself counts as one idea, so the verb is singular.
This structure is very useful in Task 2, because it lets you make an action the topic of your sentence: “Investing in education benefits everyone.”

items.text: Reading books improve your vocabulary.
Reading books improves your vocabulary.
Using phones during exams is not allowed.
Learning a new language takes time and patience.

sections.title: Rule 7: There is or there are? Look ahead
sections.label: Rule 7: There is or there are? Look ahead

paragraphs: In most sentences, the subject comes before the verb. Sentences beginning with there work differently. Here, there is only a placeholder, and the real subject appears after the verb.
So before you choose is or are (or was or were), look ahead to the noun that follows. If it is singular or uncountable, use is. If it is plural, use are.

rows: There is a lot of traffic.

items.text: There is many advantages to online learning.
There are many advantages to online learning.
There was a slight fall in sales in 2015.

sections.title: Rule 8: A number of vs. the number of
sections.label: Rule 8: A number of vs. the number of

paragraphs: These two phrases look almost identical, but they mean very different things. A number of means “many” or “several”, so the real subject is the plural noun that follows, and the verb is plural.
The number of refers to one figure, a single statistic. In this case, number itself is the head noun, so the verb is singular. You will use this second phrase constantly in Task 1 reports.

rows: A number of students have complained.
The number of students has doubled.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: “The number” is one number, so it takes a singular verb.

sections.title: Rule 9: Percentages and fractions (a Task 1 favorite)
sections.label: Rule 9: Percentages and fractions (a Task 1 favorite)

paragraphs: Percentages and fractions such as 40%, half, a third, most of and some of do not have a number of their own. Instead, they borrow it from the noun that comes after of. If that noun is singular or uncountable, use a singular verb. If it is plural, use a plural verb.
This rule matters most in Task 1, where you describe proportions in almost every sentence. Always check the noun after of before you choose the verb.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: The proportion of, the percentage of and the figure for are always singular, because the head noun is proportion, percentage or figure. ✓ The proportion of students who passed was 65%.

sections.title: Rule 10: Who, which and that point back
sections.label: Rule 10: Who, which and that point back

paragraphs: Relative pronouns such as who, which and that do not have a number of their own either. They point back to the noun just before them, and the verb inside the relative clause agrees with that noun.
When you see who, which or that, read backwards to the noun it refers to. That noun tells you whether the verb should be singular or plural.

items.text: Students who live on campus save money on transport.
A city that has good public transport is easier to live in.
Countries which has strong economies attract migrants.
Countries which have strong economies attract migrants.

blocks.title: Group nouns
paragraphs: Nouns like government, family, team, committee and council describe a group of people. In British English, these are sometimes used with a plural verb, which can be confusing. For IELTS, the safest choice is to treat them as singular and stay consistent throughout your essay.

items.text: The government has announced a new policy.
My family lives in a small town.

blocks.title: Neither…nor and either…or
paragraphs: When two subjects are joined by neither…nor or either…or, the verb agrees with the subject that is nearer to it. Look at the noun just before the verb and match the verb to that noun.

items.text: Neither the teacher nor the students were ready.
Neither the students nor the teacher was ready.

paragraphs: Here is how these rules appear in real IELTS writing. Notice how often the head noun is followed by a modifier, and how often Task 1 relies on Rules 8 and 9.

rows: The number of tourists rose sharply after 2010.
The figures for Japan and Korea were similar.
There was a slight fall in 2015.
Social media platforms have changed the way we communicate.
Investing in education benefits the whole of society.
A number of countries have already banned plastic bags.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common in IELTS essays. If you check only for these, you will already catch most of your agreement mistakes.

rows: The number of cars are increasing.
The number of cars is increasing.
One of the main reasons are cost.
One of the main reasons is cost.

paragraphs: Use this quick routine during the last few minutes of your writing test, sentence by sentence.

steps: Find the verb: is, are, was, were, has, have, or any present simple verb.
Ask: who or what is doing this? That word is the head noun.
Read the head noun and the verb together, skipping the modifier. If it sounds wrong, fix it.

furtherStudy.title: Purdue OWL: Subject-Verb Agreement
furtherStudy.description: A clear rule summary from a trusted university writing center.

cards.front: My phone battery ____ very quickly these days.
cards.why: My phone battery is one thing, so the present simple verb takes -s.

cards.front: The price of onions ____ gone up again.
cards.why: The head noun is price, not onions. “Of onions” is only a modifier, so read it as: The price has gone up.

cards.front: Sleep and exercise ____ both important before an exam.
cards.why: Two things joined by and (sleep and exercise) make a plural subject, so the verb is plural.

cards.front: Everyone in my class ____ WhatsApp to share notes.
cards.why: Everyone makes us picture many people, but grammatically it is singular, so the verb takes -s.

cards.front: The traffic in big cities ____ hours of people’s time every day.
cards.why: Traffic is an uncountable noun, so it takes a singular verb. “In big cities” is only a modifier.

cards.front: Learning ten new words a day ____ your writing.
cards.why: The subject is an activity (learning ten new words a day), and an activity counts as one idea. Words is part of the activity, not the head noun.

cards.front: There ____ a few reasons why students skip breakfast.
cards.why: After there, look ahead to the real subject. “A few reasons” is plural, so we use are.

cards.front: A number of students ____ complained about the new timetable.
cards.why: A number of means “many”, so the verb is plural. Compare: The number of students has risen.

cards.front: In 2020, 40% of the national budget ____ spent on education.
cards.why: With percentages, the verb follows the noun after of. Budget is singular, so we use was. Compare: 40% of students were female.

cards.front: Students who ____ far from campus often arrive late.
cards.why: Who points back to students, which is plural, so the verb in the relative clause is plural too.

errors.hint: What is the head noun before “of”?
errors.explanation: The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb (Rule 8).

errors.hint: Who or what makes it harder?
errors.explanation: The head noun is lack; “of face-to-face contact with colleagues” is a modifier (Rule 1).

first letter: s or f · meaning: reach a fair middle point between two things

errors.hint: What is the head noun: spending or people?
errors.explanation: Spending is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb (Rules 1 and 4).

errors.hint: Is figures singular or plural?
errors.explanation: Figures is plural, so the verb is plural (Rule 1).

blanks.hint: first letter: r or i or g · meaning: became higher
first letter: n or s · meaning: become smaller

errors.hint: How many things are joined by and?
errors.explanation: Two subjects joined by and make a plural subject (Rule 2).

errors.hint: Look at the first word of the subject.
errors.explanation: Each of takes a singular verb (Rule 3).

blanks.hint: first letter: a · meaning: easy to get
first letter: p or e · meaning: help to spread or grow

errors.hint: Does “a number of” mean one or many?
errors.explanation: A number of means “many”, so the verb is plural (Rule 8).

errors.hint: Cover “that depends on overseas income” and read again.
errors.explanation: The head noun is economy, which is singular (Rule 1).

blanks.hint: adjective · meaning: easily harmed
noun · meaning: money put into businesses to earn profit

errors.hint: The head noun is not households.
errors.explanation: The proportion of always takes a singular verb (Rule 9).

errors.hint: What does which refer back to?
errors.explanation: Which refers to regions, which is plural (Rule 10).

errors.hint: Look at the noun after there.
errors.explanation: A rise is singular, so we use there was (Rule 7).

blanks.hint: verb (past participle) · meaning: become much higher
adjective · meaning: not large

errors.hint: Is the head noun rates or cities? Either way, is it singular?
errors.explanation: The head noun is rates, which is plural (Rule 1).

errors.hint: What tends to discourage crime?
errors.explanation: The head noun is sense; “of community that exists in villages” is a modifier (Rule 1).

blanks.hint: verb · meaning: make available
noun · meaning: watching an area with cameras or police
adjective · meaning: able to work for a long time

errors.hint: Is platforms singular or plural?
errors.explanation: Platforms is plural, so the verb is plural (Rule 1).

errors.hint: What makes it difficult?
errors.explanation: The head noun is speed; “of these platforms” is a modifier (Rule 1).

errors.hint: Look at the noun after There.
errors.explanation: Concerns is plural, so we use there are (Rule 7).

blanks.hint: phrasal verb · meaning: trust and use regularly
verb · meaning: take action against
noun · meaning: the ability to judge information critically

errors.hint: Is figures singular or plural?
errors.explanation: Figures is plural, so the verb is plural (Rule 1).

errors.hint: Start from “The total number of…”.
errors.explanation: The head noun is number, which is singular (Rules 1 and 8).

blanks.hint: meaning: chosen by the largest number of travelers
meaning: moved ahead of
meaning: was different

errors.hint: Start from “The variety of…”.
errors.explanation: The head noun is variety, which is singular (Rule 1).

errors.hint: With neither…nor, check the noun nearest the verb.
errors.explanation: The nearer subject, corporations, is plural (Small note: neither…nor).

errors.hint: What does that refer back to?
errors.explanation: That refers to industries, which is plural (Rule 10).

blanks.hint: meaning: have to deal with
meaning: financial help
meaning: ways to earn a regular wage

errors.hint: Start from “A visit to…”.
errors.explanation: The head noun is visit, which is singular (Rule 1).
